## Core question

If we knew the distribution of the observable data exactly, with infinite data, could we pin
down the quantity of interest uniquely? Identifiability is a property of the **model and the
observation scheme**, not of a particular dataset or estimator.

## Definitions across fields

### Parametric statistical models

> A model $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$ is identifiable if the map $\theta \mapsto P_\theta$
> is one-to-one: $\theta_1 \neq \theta_2 \Rightarrow P_{\theta_1} \neq P_{\theta_2}$.
> [@rothenberg1971identification; @paulino1994identifiability]

### Econometrics

> The structural parameters of an economic model are identified if they can be recovered
> uniquely from the distribution of observables, classically from the reduced form.
> [@koopmans1949identification]

The word "identification" covers many distinct notions in econometrics: point, set, local,
generic, weak, and others. @lewbel2019identification surveys them.

### Causal inference

> A causal estimand is identifiable, given a causal model (e.g. a DAG) and its assumptions, if
> it can be written as a unique functional of the observed-data distribution. Every model
> consistent with the assumptions and the observed distribution must give it the same value.
> [@pearl2009causality]

Here the object being identified is an **estimand**, not necessarily a model parameter.

### Systems biology and dynamical systems

> A model is *structurally* identifiable if its parameters are uniquely determined by the
> model output under ideal conditions: noise-free, continuous observation of the measured
> outputs. [@bellman1970structural]

See [structural non-identifiability](structural-non-identifiability.qmd) and
[practical identifiability](practical-identifiability.qmd).

### Bayesian inference

Identifiability is not required for a proper posterior. With a proper prior, a nonidentified
model still gives a well-defined posterior, and the data can update beliefs about nonidentified
parameters *through* their prior dependence on identified ones. If $\theta = (\theta_I,
\theta_N)$, where the likelihood depends only on $\theta_I$, then
$p(\theta_N \mid \theta_I, y) = p(\theta_N \mid \theta_I)$: the data never update the
*conditional* prior. [@poirier1998revising; @gustafson2015bayesian]

## Formal statement

Let $\mathcal{P} = \{P_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$.

- **Global identifiability:** $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2} \Rightarrow \theta_1 = \theta_2$ for
  all $\theta_1, \theta_2 \in \Theta$.
- **Local identifiability at $\theta_0$:** the same implication holds within some open
  neighbourhood of $\theta_0$. Under regularity conditions this is equivalent to a nonsingular
  information matrix at $\theta_0$. [@rothenberg1971identification]
- **Generic identifiability:** identifiability holds everywhere except on a measure-zero
  subset of $\Theta$. [@allman2009identifiability]
- **Identifiability of a functional $\psi(\theta)$:** $P_{\theta_1} = P_{\theta_2} \Rightarrow
  \psi(\theta_1) = \psi(\theta_2)$. A functional can be identified when $\theta$ is not.

## Examples

- $Y \sim N(a + b, 1)$: $(a, b)$ is not identifiable, but $a + b$ is.
- Finite mixtures are identifiable only up to relabelling of the components.
- Misclassified binary exposure: when sensitivity and specificity are unknown, prevalence is
  not identified from the error-prone measure alone. [@gustafson2005model]

## Connections and distinctions

- **[Structural vs. practical](structural-non-identifiability.qmd):** a model can be identifiable
  in principle and still [practically non-identifiable](practical-identifiability.qmd) with
  finite, noisy data.
- **[Partial identification](partial-identification.qmd):** when point identification fails,
  the data may still restrict the quantity to a set.
- **[Recoverability](recoverability.qmd):** *(proposed)* recoverability asks which
  functionals can be learned, and may hold when the full parameter is not identifiable.
- **Observability** (control theory): whether the system state can be reconstructed from
  outputs. It is the state analogue of parameter identifiability. *(needs a reference and an
  entry)*

## Key references

- @rothenberg1971identification: global and local identification, and the information matrix.
- @koopmans1949identification: origin of the identification problem in econometrics.
- @lewbel2019identification: map of the many meanings of "identification".
- @pearl2009causality: identification of causal effects from observational distributions.
- @poirier1998revising: what Bayesian updating can and cannot do without identification.

## Open questions

- *(open)* Is there a common definition that covers parameters (statistics), estimands (causal
  inference), and states (control theory)? Or are these different questions?
- *(open)* How should "identified" be reported when it holds generically but fails at the
  parameter values that matter scientifically, e.g. at the boundary?
